steps.description: Design a numerical experiment to test if small feedforward networks can probe solution space rigidity. Define a class of analytic constraints (e.g., polynomial or trigonometric functions with known solution properties), vary the number of constraints w, and scan hidden layer widths N to find N_c(w) — the minimum width achieving zero violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out test points. Train small MLPs (1–2 hidden layers, activation=ReLU) on w constraints sampled from the target function, evaluate on a dense grid of test points, record N_c(w), and assess whether N_c remains bounded (rigid) or diverges (fat) as w increases. Use 3–5 random seeds per (w,N) for robustness.

plans.objective: [DIM: structure] If the constraints define a low-degree algebraic variety of dimension d, then the minimal width N_c(w) required to achieve zero violation on out-of-sample points is bounded by a constant independent of w, specifically N_c(w) ≤ d+1, reflecting the intrinsic dimensionality of the constraint manifold. | predict: N_c(w) remains constant (≤ 5) as w increases from 5 to 40, with out-of-sample error ≤ 1e-3 achieved at fixed width across all w. | pro: This hypothesis directly addresses the core question of whether network capacity scales with sample size or is constrained by algebraic structure; it aligns with known results in algebraic geometry where polynomial interpolation requires width proportional to degree. con: Assumes constraints are exactly polynomial; real-world constraints may involve noise or transcendental functions that break this structure.

steps.description: Design and run a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that the minimal width N_c(w) for zero violation on out-of-sample points is bounded by a constant (≤ d+1) independent of sample size w. We will: (1) construct a low-degree algebraic constraint manifold of known dimension d (e.g., a 2D polynomial surface in R^3); (2) sample w points from w=5 to 40; (3) train small feedforward networks of varying width N to interpolate training points; (4) measure out-of-sample max absolute error on held-out points; (5) determine N_c(w) as the smallest width achieving max error ≤ 1e-3. We will compare against the prediction that N_c(w) remains ≤ d+1 (e.g., ≤3) across all w. This directly tests the algebraic geometry claim about intrinsic dimensionality limiting network capacity.

plans.objective: ** The structure hypothesis (algebraic variety) because it makes the clearest prediction (constant N_c) that's easiest to test definitively - either N_c plateaus or it doesn't. This provides a binary test of rigidity vs fatness as specified in the problem statement.

steps.description: Systematically scan the capacity parameter space (hidden width N) vs constraint count w to measure N_c(w). For each w, sweep N from a lower bound (e.g., 10) to an upper bound (e.g., 200) until zero-violation is achieved (max absolute error on held-out points ≤ 1e-3). Use a small synthetic function family to generate the bootstrap constraints. Record the minimum N for each w. If N_c plateaus at a finite value as w increases, the hypothesis is supported (rigid); if N_c grows without bound or never reaches zero-violation within the scan range, the hypothesis is rejected (fat).

plans.objective: [DIM: dynamics] If the solution space is governed by a gradient flow with a sharp energy landscape, the minimal width N_c(w) required to achieve zero violation will grow logarithmically with the number of constraints w, i.e., N_c(w) ∼ log(w), reflecting the need for exponentially more capacity to resolve narrow basins of attraction in high-dimensional space.

steps.description: I will design a computational experiment to test the hypothesis that minimal network width N_c(w) grows logarithmically with constraint count w for a gradient-flow-governed solution space. The plan: (1) Define a constrained regression problem with w linear equality constraints sampled from a sharp energy landscape (e.g., high-frequency sinusoidal target with narrow basins). (2) Sweep hidden layer width N ∈ [4, 128] for each w ∈ {10, 20, 50, 100, 200}. (3) For each (w, N) triplet, train a small feedforward network (2 hidden layers, ReLU) on w constraint points and evaluate max absolute error on a held-out test set of w constraints. (4) Determine N_c(w) as the smallest N achieving zero violation (max error ≤ 1e-3). (5) Fit log(w) scaling to N_c(w) and compare against linear/exponential alternatives. This directly tests the numeric claim N_c(w) ∼ log(w) using the specified zero-violation criterion.
